concepts.heading: A Pleasure-Positive Approach to Safer Sex
concepts.plain: Harm reduction means making sex safer in real life, without shame.

concepts.heading: Why Shame-Based Approaches Fail
concepts.alt: A guide pushing away a dark storm cloud with a pointing finger inside it, looking unimpressed
concepts.plain: Scaring and shaming people does not make them safer. It makes them hide.

concepts.heading: The Harm Reduction Alternative
concepts.alt: Two guides walking side by side on a path, one holding a small first-aid kit with a heart
concepts.plain: People will have sex. Good information helps them do it more safely.

concepts.heading: The Spectrum of Safer Sex
concepts.alt: A guide sliding a marker along a long colour bar that fades from green to orange
concepts.plain: Sex is not just "safe" or "unsafe". Risk goes from lower to higher.

concepts.heading: Pleasure-Positive Framing
concepts.alt: A guide holding a heart in one hand and a shield in the other, smiling confidently
concepts.plain: Talking about safety first lets everyone relax and enjoy it more.

checks.prompt: A clinic gives people clear facts and tools without judging their choices. Which approach is this?
checks.explanation: Harm reduction. Harm reduction acknowledges that people are going to have sex — and that sex is a normal, healthy part of human life.

checks.prompt: How does harm reduction describe sexual risk?
options: As a spectrum from lower to higher
checks.explanation: As a spectrum from lower to higher. Rather than thinking of sex as either "safe" or "unsafe," harm reduction invites us to see a spectrum.

bcba76bd-16d3-4fd6-a96f-18369ea26ce4.takeaway: Safer sex works best with good information and no shame.

concepts.heading: Modern Prevention Tools and Testing Practices
Barrier Methods
concepts.alt: A guide holding a shield with a heart on it in front of him like an umbrella
concepts.plain: Condoms, dental dams and gloves block fluids. They are cheap and they work.

concepts.heading: PrEP and PEP: HIV Prevention
concepts.alt: A guide holding a pill bottle and a small calendar, a shield icon above
concepts.plain: PrEP is medicine you take before to prevent HIV. PEP is emergency medicine after.

concepts.heading: U=U: Undetectable = Untransmittable
concepts.alt: Two guides standing close with arms around each other's shoulders under a big equals sign
concepts.plain: A person on HIV treatment that works cannot pass HIV on through sex.

concepts.heading: Testing Recommendations for ENM
concepts.alt: A guide holding a calendar with a test tube icon on one day, giving a thumbs up
concepts.plain: With more than one partner, get tested regularly. Every 3 months is common.

concepts.heading: Talking About Testing
concepts.alt: Two guides talking over coffee, a speech bubble with a test tube icon and a heart between them
concepts.plain: Talking about testing feels awkward at first. A few simple lines make it easy.

concepts.heading: Destigmatizing STIs
concepts.alt: A guide peeling a dark label off a jar to show a plain medical cross underneath
concepts.plain: An STI is a health issue, not a mark on your character. Most are treatable.

checks.explanation: Undetectable equals untransmittable. This is known as U=U (Undetectable = Untransmittable).

checks.prompt: For people with multiple partners, what testing rhythm does the lesson mention as common?
checks.explanation: About every 3 months. For people with multiple partners, regular testing is an act of care for yourself and your network.

90c7413a-4271-4948-a458-e6546e98bc81.takeaway: Use barriers, know about PrEP and PEP, and get tested about every 3 months if you have more than one partner.

concepts.heading: Navigating Fluid Bonding in ENM
concepts.plain: Stopping condoms with one partner is a big decision that touches everyone.

concepts.heading: What Is Fluid Bonding?
concepts.alt: Two guides holding hands, a small droplet icon inside a heart floating between them
concepts.plain: Fluid bonding means agreeing to have sex with a certain partner without barriers.

concepts.heading: Why Fluid Bonding Matters in ENM
What to Include in a Fluid Bonding Agreement
concepts.alt: Two guides signing a shared paper on a clipboard together, a pen each
concepts.plain: A good agreement says who uses what with whom, how often you test and what happens after a slip.

concepts.heading: When New Partners Enter
concepts.alt: One welcomes a newcomer at a door while the third holds a pause sign beside a checklist
concepts.plain: A new partner means it is time to talk the agreement through again.

concepts.heading: The Emotional Dimensions
concepts.alt: A guide holding a heart close to his chest with both hands, eyes closed
concepts.plain: This is about feelings as well as health. It can mean trust and closeness.

concepts.heading: Sample Agreement Framework
concepts.plain: Write your agreement down in plain steps so no one has to guess.

options: Sex that involves sharing bodily fluids without barriers
checks.explanation: Sex that involves sharing bodily fluids without barriers. Fluid bonding refers to engaging in sexual activities that involve the exchange of bodily fluids (semen, vaginal fluid, blood) without barriers.

checks.prompt: A fluid-bonded partner starts seeing someone new. What does the lesson suggest?
options: Revisit the agreement before anything changes
checks.explanation: Revisit the agreement before anything changes. One of the most common situations that tests fluid bonding agreements is the introduction of a new sexual partner.

605941de-2545-43b4-be7e-3cdf6ab2e7d3.takeaway: Going without barriers is a shared agreement. Talk it through again when anything changes.

concepts.heading: Beyond the Binary: Sexual Health for Everyone
concepts.plain: Most sex ed was written for one kind of body. Good sex ed fits every body.

concepts.heading: Inclusive Anatomy Language
concepts.alt: A guide holding up a speech bubble with a heart and a body-outline icon, speaking kindly
concepts.plain: Use the words for body parts that the person uses for themselves.

concepts.heading: Sexual Health for Trans and Nonbinary People
concepts.alt: He talks with her, a friendly doctor in a white coat, both smiling
concepts.plain: Trans and nonbinary people have their own health needs and deserve care that fits.

concepts.heading: Pleasure and Safety for People with Disabilities
concepts.alt: A guide sitting in a wheelchair, smiling warmly, holding a heart
concepts.plain: Disabled people have sex lives too, and deserve both pleasure and safety.

concepts.heading: Age-Inclusive Sexual Health
concepts.alt: A guide with silver streaks in her purple hair, dancing joyfully with a heart above
concepts.plain: Sex does not stop at a certain age. Bodies change and so do the needs.

concepts.heading: Systemic Barriers
concepts.alt: A guide standing in front of a tall wall with a small locked door, hands on hips
concepts.plain: Some groups face extra walls to getting care, like cost, bias and distance.

concepts.heading: Finding Inclusive Providers
concepts.alt: A guide holding a map with a pin marked by a medical cross and a heart
concepts.plain: There are lists that help you find a doctor who will treat you with respect.

checks.after: Pleasure and Safety for People with Disabilities
checks.prompt: What does society often wrongly assume about people with disabilities?
options: That they have no sexual desires or needs
checks.explanation: That they have no sexual desires or needs. People with disabilities are often desexualized by society — treated as though they do not have sexual desires or needs.

checks.prompt: Does sexual health stop mattering at a certain age?
options: No, it matters at every age
checks.explanation: No, it matters at every age. Sexual health does not stop at a certain age.

1075b350-032e-404b-96e8-b4ecc37c8bc5.takeaway: Good sexual health care fits every body, age and ability.
